# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems are designed. A column of water one foot tall exerts about 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure at its base, which means that lifting water is fundamentally a fight against gravity—and one that engineers have been waging with increasing sophistication for over a century. To understand how a modern city delivers water to the fifteenth floor of an apartment building, we need to follow the water from its source, through the distribution network, and up to your faucet, watching how pressure is created, lost, and deliberately restored along the way.

## The Fundamental Currency: Hydraulic Head

Engineers describe water's energy using the concept of "head," expressed in feet of elevation. Water at the top of a reservoir 200 feet above a faucet has 200 feet of head available to push it through pipes. Every foot of elevation gained costs a foot of head; every foot lost going downhill returns it. Friction in pipes also consumes head, which is why long, narrow pipes deliver weaker pressure than short, wide ones.

This explains the classic design of older water systems: put the reservoir on a hill
